family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with opposite/decussate exstipulate leaves, then the inflorescence: spikes or compact heads are common. Confirm a tubular flower, superior ovary and usually terminal style.
family_diagnostics.flowers: Usually 4- or 5-merous, tubular and zygomorphic to weakly bilabiate.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Can split into 2 or 4 mericarps or become drupaceous, depending on genus.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Square stems and aroma do not separate Verbenaceae from Lamiaceae.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: The family lesson is really about inflorescence + style/ovary/fruit, not 'square stem versus mint.'

steps.title: 1 · Keep the Verbena spike in mind
steps.look_for: Opposite leaves and an elongated spike of small tubular flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the common local Verbena family form.

steps.title: 2 · Add capitate family breadth
steps.look_for: Woody habit with opposite rough leaves and dense rounded flower heads.
steps.why_it_matters: Shows that Verbenaceae is broader than Verbena spikes.

steps.title: 3 · See the drupaceous exception
steps.look_for: Fleshy dark drupe-like fruit rather than four dry mericarps.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents memorizing one fruit type for the family.

steps.title: 4 · Separate from Lamiaceae
steps.look_for: Verbenaceae commonly has a terminal style and less deeply lobed ovary; Lamiaceae commonly has a deeply 4-lobed ovary with gynobasic style.
steps.why_it_matters: This is far stronger than stem shape.

comparisons.title: Verbenaceae vs Lamiaceae
comparisons.rule: Do not use square stems alone. Read inflorescence architecture, ovary lobing, style position and fruit.

comparisons.title: Verbenaceae vs Rubiaceae
comparisons.rule: Rubiaceae has interpetiolar stipules and an inferior ovary; Verbenaceae lacks stipules and has a superior ovary.

visual_lesson.caveat: The canonical Verbena photo lock is still pending; the current visual module is scientifically usable but not visually complete.

family_confusion_cleanup.field_question: Opposite leaves and a tubular flower: mint, verbena, or madder/coffee family?
look_here_first: At the node: are there interpetiolar stipules between opposite leaves?
At the ovary: is it inferior, or superior and deeply lobed?
At fruiting: four nutlets, a drupe/schizocarp, or a capsule/berry-like fruit?
Use square stems and aroma only as supporting clues.

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Opposite/decussate leaves usually without stipules; stems often 4-angled and foliage often aromatic.
comparison_matrix.break_the_tie: Superior ovary commonly deeply 4-lobed with a gynobasic style; fruit commonly four nutlets.
comparison_matrix.exception: Not every mint is aromatic, square-stemmed, bilabiate, or four-nutleted; Callicarpa is a conspicuous local breadth exception.

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Opposite leaves and often 4-angled stems can mimic Lamiaceae closely.
comparison_matrix.break_the_tie: Do not stop at the stem. Inspect ovary/style/fruit architecture; the classic deeply 4-lobed gynobasic mint ovary is not the default verbena pattern.
comparison_matrix.exception: Family boundaries historically shifted, so older references may place some genera differently.

comparison_matrix.first_lock: Opposite or whorled leaves can mimic mints/verbena vegetatively.
comparison_matrix.break_the_tie: Look BETWEEN opposite petioles for interpetiolar stipules, then confirm an inferior ovary when flowers/fruit allow.
comparison_matrix.exception: In Galium and relatives stipules can look leaflike, making the node appear whorled rather than simply opposite.

decision_key: Opposite leaves: inspect the node before the flower.
Distinct interpetiolar stipule or stipular sheath between petioles? → strong Rubiaceae door; seek inferior ovary confirmation.
No stipules: inspect the ovary/style and later fruit.
Deeply four-lobed superior ovary + style arising among/between lobes + four nutlets → strong Lamiaceae door.
Opposite-leaved Lamiales look-alike without that mint ovary/fruit package → keep Verbenaceae and other Lamiales open until reproductive characters resolve it.

family_confusion_visual_polish.scope: Existing 14-taxon / five-genus Master Plant Pool; recognition/confusion polish only, not a species taxonomy or native-range review.
family_confusion_visual_polish.field_question: Opposite leaves, small tubular flowers and a four-angled stem: how do I prove Verbenaceae instead of a mint, Rubiaceae or another Lamiales family?
look_here_first: At a mature leaf node, look for opposite/decussate leaves without interpetiolar stipules; this is a first-pass clue, not proof.

Trace one flower to the ovary and style: in common Verbenaceae the ovary is superior, generally not deeply four-lobed externally, and the style is terminal; contrast the deeply four-lobed, often gynobasic mint ovary.

Inspect a mature fruit WITH its persistent calyx: determine whether it divides into four dry mericarps, two dry mericarps, or is a fleshy drupe. Fruit architecture gives stronger genus routing than flower color.
Read inflorescence structure: elongate spike/panicle of spikes, short contracted head, creeping pedunculate head, woody raceme, or woody head.

comparison_matrix.similarity: Opposite exstipulate leaves, tubular/bilabiate flowers, frequently four-angled stems; both may produce four nutlet-like units.
comparison_matrix.separate: Dissect the superior ovary before fruiting: typical mint has four conspicuous lobes with gynobasic style, while typical verbena-family ovary is less deeply lobed with terminal style. Compare mature mericarps and calyx; fruit count alone can mislead.
comparison_matrix.exceptions: Callicarpa is in Lamiaceae despite its drupaceous fruit; not every mint has a gynobasic style. Do not use scent or square stem as a family key.

comparison_matrix.similarity: Opposite leaves and sometimes clustered small tubular flowers; Cephalanthus heads can resemble Verbenaceae heads at a distance.
comparison_matrix.separate: At the node find interpetiolar stipules; confirm inferior Rubiaceae ovary beneath floral parts. Verbenaceae generally lacks stipules and has a superior ovary.
comparison_matrix.exceptions: Galium stipules can resemble extra whorled leaves. Rubiaceae fruits are diverse; avoid using fruit fleshiness alone.

comparison_matrix.similarity: Lamiales with opposite leaves and tubular flowers; a small spike can resemble Verbena.
comparison_matrix.separate: Plantaginaceae commonly has many-seeded capsules; Acanthaceae often has two-valved capsules with retinacula (seed-support hooks), though not universally. Verbenaceae typically has mericarps or drupaceous fruits, not those capsule mechanisms.
comparison_matrix.exceptions: Fruit and stamen patterns vary; dissect the actual local specimen rather than treating a single character as universal.

five_genus_routing.door: Usually erect/ascending herbs with elongate terminal spikes or panicles of spikes; persistent calyx encloses a dry fruit separating into four one-seeded mericarps.
five_genus_routing.compare: Glandularia generally has a shorter, contracted head and relatively long style; Verbena spikes may be compact when young. Confirm fruit and mature inflorescence.

five_genus_routing.door: Often lower, spreading herbs with compact terminal flower heads/spikes; deeply divided leaves common in local taxa; dry fruit separates into four mericarps.
five_genus_routing.compare: Versus Verbena, compare contracted unbranched heads, style relative to ovary and leaf division; no single vegetative character is sufficient.

five_genus_routing.door: Prostrate/creeping stems often rooting at nodes, pedunculate dense heads of very small flowers; fruit divides into TWO dry mericarps.
five_genus_routing.compare: Versus Lantana, check herbaceous creeping nodes and dry two-part fruit rather than woody shoots and fleshy drupe; versus Glandularia, compare flower size, leaf division and fruit count.

five_genus_routing.door: Woody shrub with rough opposite leaves and compact rounded/flattened heads; fruit matures as a fleshy drupe with a hard stone/pyrene.
five_genus_routing.compare: A flower head alone can mimic Phyla; follow to woody stem and mature fleshy fruit. Lantana species/hybrid identities are separate taxonomy-review work.

five_genus_routing.door: Woody aromatic shrubs with opposite or sometimes whorled leaves and small tubular flowers in relatively narrow spikes/racemes; fruit is a dry schizocarp, often two nutlet-like mericarps.
five_genus_routing.compare: Unlike Lantana, usually elongated flowering axes and dry rather than fleshy fruit; unlike Verbena, persistent woody branching. Scent is supporting, never decisive.

teaching_cautions: Four dry mericarps are not unique to Verbenaceae: mints often yield four nutlets; inspect ovary/style architecture and other characters.
A head is an inflorescence, not one flower; dissect a single small corolla and calyx from the head.
Some older references place Callicarpa, Vitex or other former Verbenaceae members in this family; modern treatments place these in Lamiaceae.
Do not infer native status from inclusion in Master Plant Pool. Encounter/comparison taxa remain in the learner with existing status labels.
